properties.decision:
**RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.** Anthony, 2026-08-26, thinking out loud after the third instance of one defect class landed in a single week.

His words: *"we do some type of classing or typing of skills/tools? like read vs write could be one kind. there are probably other types. then do some standardization of what each of those types skills/tools needs and make sure all the type has those same required attributes for its type?"*

📌 DISTINCT FROM `dec:idea-a-proposed-decision-asserts-nothing-so-what-may-a-structural-detector-say-about-it`, which the guard offered: that one is an ANSWERED question about one status and three finding kinds. This asks what a declared KIND obliges of its members in general, and it outlives that instance.

═══ ⭐ THE PREMISE IS HALF-TRUE, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS THE INTERESTING PART ═══

Measured on the served surface 2026-08-26, over **173 declared tools**:

| axis | declared on | |
|---|---|---|
| `read_only_hint` | **161** (93%) | the read/write class ALREADY EXISTS and is near-uniform |
| `destructive_hint` | **7** (4%) | |
| `idempotent_hint` | **1** (0.6%) | |
| `open_world_hint` | **0** | |
| `title` | 9 (5%) | |

**And ZERO of them are checked by anything** — no Python gate, no Rust test, nothing in `toolsnap.py` reads any of these annotations. So the 93% is a HABIT, not a construction. The 12 tools declaring nothing at all are invisible to everything, and a 174th declaring nothing would be equally invisible.

⇒ So the live question is not *"should tools be classed"* — they are. It is **whether a declared kind obliges its members to state the same things, and whether anything checks.** On today's evidence the answer to both halves is no.

📌 A SECOND OBSERVATION FROM THE SAME SWEEP, offered as a lead rather than a finding: **6 tools in the `query` slice declare `read_only_hint = false`.** That may be entirely correct — a query that records a confirmation is not read-only — but the slice NAME and the read/write CLASS disagree there, and a per-class contract is exactly the thing that would make somebody say which is wrong.

═══ WHY THIS ARRIVED NOW ═══

Anthony: *"for instance, you just found a whole class of issues. this isn't the first time this has occurred in this development... too many times, we've discovered more when we have peeled back the layers of the onion."*

Three instances inside one week, each a rule maintained by hand with nothing checking it: `unallocated_component` never read a parking ruling though two siblings did; F-01's replay contract was stated in a doc comment and enforced field by field; and three defect detectors never read `proposed` though a fourth did. The fix each time was per-instance. `chg:unallocated-component-reads-the-ruling` predicted the recurrence in writing and was right within a day.

═══ OPTIONS, none chosen ═══

**(a) A CONTRACT PER AXIS, checked by the existing lint.** `skill_lint.py` is already 1126 lines enforcing both directions between served tools and skills, and verbatim phrases that must survive rewording. Extend it: every `#[tool]` must declare the full annotation set. ⚠️ Counter: it is another hand-maintained list in a file that is already the biggest hand-maintained list in the repo — the disease treating itself.

**(b) COMPILE-TIME, the shape used twice in `heal.rs` today.** `every_category_is_listed_in_all` and the new `every_category_states_whether_it_reads_proposed` are exhaustive matches: a new variant cannot compile until its author has answered. ⚠️ Counter: works for a closed enum, and the tool surface is 173 proc-macro attributes rather than an enum. Whether the same trick reaches them is an open technical question, not a given.

**(c) LEAVE READ/WRITE ALONE AND CLASS BY SOMETHING ELSE.** Read/write is near-uniform already, so the payoff is in the axes nobody fills. ⚠️ Counter: which axes? Naming them is the actual work, and this option quietly assumes it is done.

**(d) DO NOTHING AND KEEP FIXING INSTANCES.** ⚠️ Counter: three in a week, each predicted by the last. But stated honestly — the per-instance fixes were cheap, correct, and each left a pin behind. The class fix is speculative until somebody shows a fourth instance it would have caught.

═══ ⚠️ THE HONEST COUNTERWEIGHT, WHICH IS ANTHONY'S OWN ═══

He watches for over-engineering from the acquisitions side. A per-class contract with a registry, a factory and a validator is exactly the shape an engineer reaches for and exactly the shape he distrusts. **The cheapest thing that would have caught all three instances is probably not a taxonomy — it is one test per class saying "every member answers this question", which is what `heal.rs` now does twice.** That is option (b) at its smallest, and it needs no new vocabulary at all.
properties.name: OPEN — the tool class already exists and carries no contract: should a declared kind oblige its members to state the same things, checked?
properties.rationale:
Recorded as its own question because it asks what a declared KIND obliges, which is separate from whether the three legs were applied uniformly (a specific contract) and from whether construction should go through a factory (a mechanism). Answering any one of those does not answer the others.

The measurement was taken BEFORE the options were written, and it moved the question: the first framing assumed tools were unclassed, and `read_only_hint` at 93% says otherwise. What is missing is not the class but the obligation and the check — the same shape as `fact:vocabulary-needs-three-legs-and-a-users-project-gets-none-of-it`, where a leg can be present and still deliver nothing.
